title: Make Haste, O God, to Deliver Me
superscription: For the choirmaster. Of David. To bring remembrance.

verses.text: Make haste, O God, to deliver me! Hurry, O LORD, to help me!
May those who seek my life be ashamed and confounded; may those who wish me harm be repelled and humiliated.
May those who say, "Aha, aha!" retreat because of their shame.
May all who seek You rejoice and be glad in You; may those who love Your salvation always say, "Let God be magnified!"
But I am poor and needy; hurry to me, O God. You are my help and my deliverer; O LORD, do not delay.

context.author: The title names David. In Book Two, Psalms 51-65 and 68-70 are “of David.”
context.genre: Psalm: a song or prayer in Hebrew poetry
context.audience: Israel at worship in Jerusalem, and every reader who prays
context.setting: This short psalm is almost word for word the last five verses of Psalm 40, used as a prayer on its own. “Make haste, O God, to deliver me! Hurry, O LORD, to help me!” (v.1). David asks that those who seek his life and mock him with “Aha, aha!” be turned back in shame (vv.2-3), and that all who seek God rejoice and say, “Let God be magnified!” (v.4). He ends: “But I am poor and needy; hurry to me, O God. You are my help and my deliverer; O LORD, do not delay” (v.5).
context.custom: “To bring remembrance” (title) may connect the psalm with the memorial portion of an offering (Leviticus 2:2), or mean simply a prayer asking God to remember. Psalm 38 has the same note. The monks of the early church used v.1 as a constant short prayer; John Cassian (about AD 420) recommended it for every need.
context.timelineImmediate: Psalm 71 is the prayer of an old man: “Do not discard me in my old age.”
context.timelineBible: Psalm 40:13-17 contains nearly the same words, with “the LORD” where Psalm 70 often has “God.” The opening words became the start of the daily offices in Western churches: ‘O God, come to my aid; O Lord, make haste to help me.’ Hebrews invites us to find “grace to help us in our time of need” (Hebrews 4:16).

translation.meaning: To rescue, deliver, bring to safety.

gospelParallels.note: Grace to help us in our time of need.
Will He delay in helping them?
My grace is sufficient for you.

otBackground.note: I will help you; I will uphold you.

overview.summary: A short, urgent prayer, the same as the end of Psalm 40: hurry to help me, turn back my mockers, let all who seek You rejoice; I am poor and needy.
overview.settingLine: A cry with no time to spare.

archaeology.t: Small portions burned on the altar.
Desert monks’ cells in Egypt and Judea where such prayers were repeated.

overview.discussion: “O LORD, do not delay” (v.5). Do I feel free to pray this urgently? Why or why not?
overview.book: The book of Psalms · 150 psalms (all 150 in the app). Israel’s songs and prayers: praise, lament, thanks, trust and wisdom, many of them by David.
overview.author: David
